significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish that in-context repetition "monotonically inflates" internally decoded belief for both true and false propositions, while a causally separable "familiarity/fluency" component carries this shift and can be ablated without erasing truth representation. The dose-response and truth-independence constitute a form-(iii) law that predicts the ordering of belief readouts across repetition counts and truth values, while the ablatable component adds a form-(ii) causal decomposition; this would require latent-truth approaches such as Burns et al.'s Discovering Latent Knowledge Without Supervision and Li et al.'s Inference-Time Intervention to distinguish familiarity-driven confidence from truth tracking. It establishes both a behavioral/internal phenomenon and a mechanism; the determinate negative branches are also useful, because absence of a false-claim dose-response rules out the proposed illusory-truth law, whereas an effect without a separable component supports an entangled or distributed account. In the topic-substitution check, replacing these specific repetition, dose-response, and dissociation assertions with the generic LLM-beliefs topic would not retain this score: the constraining law and two-part causal account are materially stronger than the median belief-direction hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "per-count belief/confidence dose-response slopes," the "repetition-inflation direction," and an intervention where "ablating that component restores truth-tracking." The internal slope can flag a repetition-inflated context before the model issues its truth judgment, and the ablation is an ex-ante control with an action window rather than merely a post-hoc explanation. After model-specific re-extraction, the substantive prediction still travels as a relation—belief should rise monotonically with repetition independently of truth—and the asserted scope includes "across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and repetition types," although the claim expressly leaves very large closed models uncertain. Auditors and retrieval/deployment practitioners could use the relation to identify redundant-context bias and the intervention to gate or suppress it; the topic-substitution check does not preserve this reach because generic research on LLM beliefs supplies neither the forward-looking repetition diagnostic nor the control knob.
